text: A total lunar eclipse occurred at the Moon’s descending node of orbit on Monday, April 24, 1967, with an umbral magnitude of 1.3356. This event took place when the Moon moved into Earth's shadow, causing it to be darkened, and specifically, the Moon's near side completely passed into Earth's umbral shadow, defining a total lunar eclipse. Unlike solar eclipses, which are visible only in a small region, a lunar eclipse can be observed from anywhere on the night side of Earth. A total lunar eclipse can last up to nearly two hours, whereas a total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes at any given location due to the smaller size of the Moon's shadow. Occurring just 16 hours after perigee on April 23, 1967, at 20:00 UTC, the Moon’s apparent diameter was larger. This eclipse was the first in a tetrad, a series of four total lunar eclipses occurring consecutively, with the others on October 18, 1967; April 13, 1968; and October 6, 1968. The Surveyor 3 probe was active on the Moon during this eclipse. It was completely visible over northeast Asia, Australia, and much of the Pacific Ocean, rising over most of Asia and setting over North America and western and central South America. This eclipse is part of an eclipse season, which occurs roughly every six months and lasts about 35 days, repeating every 173 days; two or three eclipses typically happen during each season, with each eclipse separated by a fortnight. It is also part of a semester series, repeating approximately every 177 days and 4 hours at alternating nodes of the Moon’s orbit. The penumbral lunar eclipse on August 27, 1969, occurs in the next lunar year eclipse set. The Metonic cycle, repeating nearly every 19 years, aligns the Earth's shadow with the same calendar date and background stars. This eclipse belongs to Saros series 121, which repeats every 18 years, 11 days, and contains 82 events, beginning with a penumbral lunar eclipse on October 6, 1047, and ending with a penumbral eclipse on March 18, 2508. The series includes partial eclipses from May 10, 1408 to July 3, 1498; total eclipses from July 13, 1516 to May 26, 2021; and a second set of partial eclipses from June 6, 2039 to August 11, 2147. The longest duration of totality occurred in member 43 on October 18, 1660, lasting 100 minutes and 29 seconds. All eclipses in this Saros series occur at the Moon’s descending node. Eclipses are tabulated in three columns, with every third eclipse in the same column being one exeligmos apart, meaning they cast shadows over similar parts of Earth. This eclipse is part of a tritos cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 135 synodic months (≈ 3986.63 days, or 11 years minus 1 month), with irregular appearances due to lack of synchronization with the anomalistic month, though groupings of three tritos cycles (≈ 33 years minus 3 months) show similar eclipses. It is also part of the long period inex cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 358 synodic months (≈ 10,571.95 days, or 29 years minus 20 days), with irregular appearances due to lack of synchronization with the anomalistic month, but groupings of three inex cycles (≈ 87 years minus 2 months) show similar eclipses. A lunar eclipse is typically preceded and followed by solar eclipses by 9 years and 5.5 days (a half saros), and this lunar eclipse is related to two annular solar eclipses of Solar Saros 128.
